Differences from the official iCARE

Source: vignettes/differences.Rmd
differences.Rmd

This package is an unofficial, refactored distribution of iCARE. The official package is maintained by its authors and distributed by Bioconductor (source: git.bioconductor.org/packages/iCARE, mirrored at github.com/bioc/iCARE), with a development repository at github.com/parichoy/iCARE.

This article lists every difference from the official version 1.40.0 that a user can notice. The functions, their arguments and the names of their results are unchanged, so existing scripts run as before; what changes is that known defects are fixed, a few outputs are added or corrected, and the figures are redrawn. Several fixes were first made in iCARE 1.33.1.9002, a patched development version prepared by the maintainer of this distribution; they are marked (1.33.1.9002).

At a glance

Area Change
Implementation Vectorized R throughout; the C code and the use.c.code option are removed; faster than the official compiled code on every benchmark
Reference weights Used correctly in the calibration of the baseline hazard (1.33.1.9002)
Ages Fractional start ages and interval lengths are used exactly
Rates Only the ages inside the intervals need rates: a missing rate where an interval ends no longer gives NA or bin-averaged risks
Incidence rates Rates by age band (three-column tables) are read as yearly rates
Missing risk factors The profile’s own observed risk factors are kept, as in the published method, instead of being replaced by the donors’
Missing risk factors: intervals Each profile’s risk uses its own interval and does not depend on the other profiles (1.33.1.9002)
Family history with SNPs Its log relative risk is attenuated in every coding of the covariate
SNP profiles Columns named after the SNPs are matched by name, not by position
SNP-only reference risks refs.risk holds the risks of simulated people, no longer averages of five people
Split intervals Competing mortality before the cut age is accounted for; reference weights are kept after it (1.33.1.9002)
AUC Tied risk scores count 1/2 (1.33.1.9002); O(n log n) time and O(n) memory
Risk groups Ties, empty groups and cut-offs are handled, and the tests’ degrees of freedom follow the groups formed (1.33.1.9002)
Cases diagnosed at exit Kept when ages have decimals, despite rounding error
Hosmer-Lemeshow test Variance under the null hypothesis by default; the earlier statistic is an option
E/O in sampled data The confidence interval accounts for the variability of E
Study incidence Person-time rates by attained age, with confidence intervals
Results Numeric group results with E/O and counts; new E/O per group with confidence intervals
Figures Redrawn with ggplot2: square panels with their statistics, publication-ready
Messages Clear errors and warnings; nothing printed to the console

The sections below give the details.

Implementation and interface

  • No compiled code. The package is written in vectorized R. The C code of the official package and the use.c.code argument are removed; computeAbsoluteRisk(use.c.code = 1) still runs, with a deprecation warning, and the setting is ignored. Every workload of the benchmark is faster than the official version with its compiled code (see vignette("performance", package = "iCARE")), and installing the package needs no compiler.
  • Dependencies. plotrix, gtools and Hmisc are no longer needed; the figures use ggplot2 (3.5.0 or later) and patchwork.
  • Model built once. When ModelValidation() computes risks for the study and for the reference population, the model (including the simulated SNP genotypes) is built once and shared, instead of once per call.
  • Methods. Results have print(), summary() and plot() methods: results of computeAbsoluteRisk() (class "icare") and computeAbsoluteRiskSplitInterval() (class "icareSplit") print a compact table and plot the distribution of the risks; results of ModelValidation() (class "icareValid") print a report that fits in 80 columns and plot with plotModelValidation().
  • Calibration attribute. The result of computeAbsoluteRisk() carries the calibrated baseline hazard (attr(result, "calibration")).
  • Messages. Invalid inputs stop with errors that name the argument and the problem (for example, the ages missing from an incidence table). The official ModelValidation() printed messages with print(); this version prints nothing and uses warnings and errors.

Absolute risks: computeAbsoluteRisk()

  • Reference weights in the calibration (1.33.1.9002). The official version filled the subject-by-age weight matrix of the baseline-hazard calibration by row, which scrambled non-uniform model.ref.dataset.weights across subjects and ages. Every risk computed with reference weights was therefore miscalibrated (uniform weights, the default, were not affected). The baseline hazard now solves the calibration equation with each subject’s own weight; with integer weights it equals the hazard obtained by replicating each reference row as many times as its weight.
  • Fractional ages. The official version needed whole-number start ages (a fractional start such as 60.5 was treated as 61 when mixed with whole ages, and stopped with an error otherwise) and counted any fraction of a year at the end of an interval as a whole year (intervals of 2.1 and 2.5 years gave the 3-year risk). Here, the time spent in each year of age is used exactly: a fraction of a year contributes that fraction of the year’s hazard.
  • Rates at the end of an interval. The official version also read the rates at the age where an interval ends, an age the interval does not include, and multiplied them by zero. A missing (NA) rate there, such as the example mortality rates from age 85 on, therefore made the risks NA (NA times 0 is NA). Worse, when the profiles had different intervals and any of them ended at such an age, every profile with complete risk factors got NA and was then silently treated as if its risk factors were missing: its risk and linear predictor became averages over its percentile bin of the reference population. Rates are now needed only for the years of age inside the intervals, and a missing one is reported with the ages concerned.
  • Rates by age band. Incidence and mortality tables with three columns (first age, last age, rate) were misread by the official version, which divided each band’s rate among the ages of the band: each year of a 5-year band got a fifth or a sixth of the yearly rate. Each year of age now gets the band’s rate.
  • Missing risk factors use the profile’s own interval (1.33.1.9002). For profiles with missing risk factors, the official version computed the reference risks of the percentile bins over the interval of the profiles as a whole (unique(apply.age.start) over all profiles), which was wrong whenever profiles had different intervals, and gave every profile with all risk factors missing the risk over the first profile’s interval. Each profile now gets the risk over its own interval, and a profile’s risk does not depend on which other profiles are computed with it.
  • Missing risk factors: the profile’s own observed values. For a profile with missing risk factors, iCARE estimates the average risk over the values the missing risk factors take given the observed ones (Pal Choudhury et al. 2020, equation 3). The donors are the reference rows in the profile’s percentile bin of the linear predictor of the observed risk factors, and the paper averages “the risks obtained from multiple filled-in values” of the profile’s risk score. The official code instead averaged the donors’ own complete-data risks, which replaces the profile’s observed risk factors by the donors’. All profiles in a bin then got the same risk and linear predictor. The estimate missed its target wherever the bins are wide, as in the tails of the risk distribution, and differed from the complete-data risk even when the missing risk factors had no effect. The risk now combines the profile’s own observed risk factors with each donor’s values of the missing ones, including in interactions between an observed and a missing risk factor. The linear predictor is the profile’s observed part plus the donors’ average missing part. In the example model, we set 15% of each risk factor to missing, at random, for 2,000 women of the reference dataset. For the 1,751 women left with a missing risk factor, the 30-year risks changed by 0.3% (median), and by more than 10% for 8.5% of them. A woman with high-risk levels of all her risk factors and an unknown BMI now gets a 30-year risk of 54%, against 58% with her BMI known; the official version gave her 25%. Risks of profiles with complete risk factors are unchanged.
  • Family history with SNPs. The SNPs explain part of the familial risk, so the log relative risk of family history is attenuated when SNPs are in the model. The attenuation applies to the effect of family history in any coding of the covariate, including a factor whose reference level is “1” (design column famhist0), for which the official version stops with an error.
  • SNP columns matched by name. The official version took the columns of apply.snp.profile in the order of model.snp.info, whatever their names. Columns named after the SNPs are now matched by name, so their order does not matter; unnamed columns are still taken in order, and naming only some of the SNPs is an error.
  • SNP-only reference risks. For a model with SNPs only, the official refs.risk averaged the risks of the n.imp sets of simulated people position by position. Since the people of different sets are unrelated, each value was an average of five people’s risks, and the distribution was far too narrow (in the example, a standard deviation of 0.013 instead of 0.030 for the 30-year risk). refs.risk now holds the risks of the first set of 10,000 simulated people, a sample from the population distribution. For models with covariates and SNPs, each reference row’s risk is averaged over its own simulated genotype sets, as before.
  • Single profiles. A single profile with a model of continuous covariates only failed in the official version (“non-conformable arguments”); it works here.
  • Design checks. Formulas whose transformations give infinite or undefined values (for example log(0)) stop with an error naming the rows, instead of producing wrong risks.

Split intervals: computeAbsoluteRiskSplitInterval()

  • Competing mortality before the cut age. The official version combined the risks before and after the cut age as AR1+(1−AR1)AR2AR_1 + (1 - AR_1) AR_2, which assumes that everyone free of the disease at the cut age is alive. This version uses AR1+S1AR2AR_1 + S_1 AR_2, where S1S_1 is the probability of reaching the cut age alive and free of the disease. The official formula overstates the risk, more so at older ages. With the same model on both sides and a whole-number cut age, the split risk now equals the risk over the whole interval.
  • Reference weights after the cut (1.33.1.9002). When no second reference dataset is given, the second model reuses the reference dataset and its weights; the official version dropped the weights.
  • return.refs.risk (1.33.1.9002) is passed on when there is a single model.

Model validation: ModelValidation()

Corrections

  • Ties in the AUC (1.33.1.9002). The official AUC counted a case and a non-case with the same risk score as discordant (0 instead of 1/2), which biases the AUC down when scores are tied, as they often are for questionnaire-based scores.
  • Exact risks for the study subjects. Because of the defect with rates at the end of an interval (above), when ModelValidation() computed the risks of the example studies, which follow women up to age 85, the official version replaced each subject’s risk and risk score by the average over her percentile bin: the 5,285 women of the nested case-control study had only 101 distinct risk scores. The risks and scores are now exact; on that study the AUC is 0.592 instead of 0.587 (with the ties of the averaged scores also counted as 0).
  • Settings of the model object (1.33.1.9002). model.ref.dataset.weights and n.imp given in iCARE.model.object are used (the official version ignored them), settings left out take the defaults of computeAbsoluteRisk(), and objects without return.lp or return.refs.risk no longer fail.
  • Supplied risks are kept (1.33.1.9002). When predicted.risk or linear.predictor is supplied, only the missing one is computed; the official version recomputed both, silently overwriting a supplied risk.
  • Onsets after exit (1.33.1.9002). A case whose onset is recorded after exit is censored at exit, now consistently in all statistics, and with a warning.
  • Cases diagnosed at exit. Onsets are compared with the follow-up up to rounding error. When follow-up ends at diagnosis and ages are recorded as decimals, the follow-up computed as exit minus entry can fall just below the recorded onset time (in floating point, 70.94 - 61.71 < 9.23). The official version then turned the case into a non-case, silently: in simulated data with ages to two decimals, it dropped nearly half of such cases.
  • Risk-score groups (1.33.1.9002). Groups are formed at (weighted) quantiles of the risk score, with the repairs needed for tied scores: values tied at a quantile form their own group instead of stopping with “breaks are not unique”, and no subject is left without a group (in the official weighted branch, rounding could drop the subjects with the lowest or highest score). Empty groups are dropped, and the degrees of freedom of the Hosmer-Lemeshow test (GG) and of the relative-risk test (G−1G - 1) follow the number of groups GG actually formed; the official version always used number.of.percentiles. Duplicated linear.predictor.cutoffs are merged, and cut-offs outside the range of the scores are ignored.
  • Reference population. reference.entry.age and reference.exit.age may give one window per reference row (the official version used the first row’s window for all), the reference weights are used, and with SNPs the reference risk score is each row’s own linear predictor averaged over its simulated genotype sets (the official version computed it as if every SNP were missing).
  • Study incidence. The official study incidence at age aa was the proportion of subjects, among those who entered at least a year before aa and were followed past aa, with onset in [a,a+1)[a, a + 1). It ignored the first year of follow-up and follow-up ending within the year. The study incidence is now the person-time rate: onsets at each year of attained age divided by the person-years lived at that age, on the scale of the population incidence rates, with 95% confidence intervals (exact Poisson intervals in a full cohort, Wald intervals with a sampling term in a sampled study) and the numbers of cases and person-years. Study_Incidence_Rate is a data frame whose first two columns, ages and study_incidence, are those of the official matrix, followed by lower, upper, cases and person_years.
  • p-values are computed in the upper tail, so very small p-values are reported instead of 0, and the htest objects describe their data (“observed and expected risks in 10 risk-score groups”).

Changed statistics

  • Hosmer-Lemeshow variance. The official statistic divided each group’s squared difference by the variance of the observed risk, Og(1−Og)/NgO_g(1 - O_g)/N_g. With few cases per group that test rejects well-calibrated models too often, and a group without cases makes it infinite. In simulations with perfectly calibrated risks and 10 groups of about 10 cases, it rejected 21.8% of the time at the 5% level. The default is now the variance under the null hypothesis of calibration, Eg(1−Eg)/NgE_g(1 - E_g)/N_g, as in the classical Hosmer-Lemeshow test; it rejected 5.6% of the time in the same simulations (see “How well the intervals and tests work” in vignette("model-validation")). hosmer.lemeshow.variance = "observed" gives the official statistic.
  • E/O confidence interval in sampled data. In a nested case-control or other sampled study, EE is a weighted sample mean, so it varies with the sample and covaries with OO. The official interval treated EE as known. The variance of log⁡(E/O)\log(E/O) now includes both, through the linearization ui=(pi/E−yi/O)/Nu_i = (p_i/E - y_i/O)/N; depending on the data, the interval can be wider or narrower. Intervals in a full cohort are unchanged.

New results and checks

  • Category_Results has numeric columns (the official ones were character strings) and adds each group’s E/O ratio with its 95% confidence interval and its numbers of subjects and cases. The E/O ratios are also returned as Category_Specific_Expected_to_Observed_Ratio.
  • Risk_Prediction_Interval is a single label, e.g. "5 years", "Observed Followup" or, for subject-specific intervals, "Subject-specific (2 to 5 years)".
  • dataset and model.name are stored with the results and used by print() and plotModelValidation().
  • Input checks: an error when no interval is given (neither predicted.risk.interval nor total.followup.validation = TRUE); cases must have a finite time of onset, while non-cases may have Inf or NA; unknown names in iCARE.model.object are reported with a warning; the settings use.c.code, return.lp and return.refs.risk of earlier model objects are accepted and ignored.

Figures: plotModelValidation()

The official figure drew five base-graphics panels, with flattened calibration plots and the statistics in a separate text panel, and returned NULL. The new figure

  • is drawn with ggplot2 and patchwork and returned as an object that can be modified and saved with ggplot2::ggsave();
  • has square panels, and the calibration panels have the same limits on both axes, so the line of perfect calibration runs at 45 degrees;
  • shows each panel’s statistics with it: E/O and the Hosmer-Lemeshow test with the absolute-risk calibration, the relative-risk test with the relative-risk calibration, the AUC with the discrimination panel;
  • compares the incidence of the study and of the population by attained age, with the study’s confidence intervals, on a log scale (the official panel compared a loess-smoothed population curve with the raw study proportions);
  • offers an optional panel of the E/O ratio of each risk-score group with its confidence interval (panels = "eo"), and a choice of panels;
  • weights the risk-score densities of a sampled study by the inverse inclusion probabilities;
  • has a title, a subtitle describing the study, and a caption explaining the points, bars and tests.

The arguments of the official function keep their meaning, except risk.score.plot.percent.smooth, which is accepted and ignored. panels, base.size and draw are new.

What stays the same

  • The functions, their arguments, and the names and meaning of their results, except where listed above.
  • The model: yearly hazards, the calibration of the baseline hazard, the simulation of SNP genotypes (with family history), and the donors for missing risk factors: the reference rows in the profile’s percentile bin (100 unweighted bins of the observed linear predictor; the averages over donors are weighted).
  • Results that were not affected by a defect agree with the official version to rounding error: the test suite compares risks, linear predictors and validation statistics with recorded outputs of the official version 1.40.0 and of 1.33.1.9002.
  • When ModelValidation() computes the risks itself, each subject’s risk covers her follow-up within the interval, as before; supply predicted.risk to validate fixed-horizon risks.
  • The risk score of the AUC and of the risk groups is the linear predictor, which excludes age.
